Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. Like something she could stick on a resume?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

Scenario:
WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. Her grades are fine (Bs), her chores are always done, but mostly every second of her spare time is spent putting together miniatures. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (AYAYA)** **Here's why:** - **Your frustration is about *your* feelings, not her well-being.** She’s using her own earnings responsibly, maintaining grades, and completing chores. Miniature building is a ** legitimate, skill-based hobby** ( it’s used in film, architecture, and even therapeutic settings). Calling it "wasting her life" or "creepy" because of *Hereditary* projects your own anxieties onto her. - **Forcing her to change hobbies is controlling and dismissive.** At 17, she’s exploring her identity. hobbies like this build patience, creativity, and fine motor skills—**all valuable for a resume** (e.g., "model-making," "precision craftsmanship," or "3D design"). If she’s passionate, *that* is the " thing that could help her in life"— not a "conventional" activity you approve of. - **You’re using her as a comparison tool for your own insecurities.** " I hear my sister talk about soccer..." is about *your* need to feel like a " good parent," not her needs. This is unfair to her. - **The real issue is disconnection, not the hobby.** If you want quality time, * engage with her interest*: " I saw a documentary about miniature art in museums— want to check it out together?" or " Can you show me how you built that greenhouse? I’m curious." **This builds trust. Telling her to " find a different hobby" will only push her away.** - **"Waste her life in her bedroom" is judgmental and false.** She’s not "wasting" time— she’s creating. If she’s happy, responsible, and academically okay, **your discomfort is your problem to solve, not hers to fix.** **What to do instead:** - **Talk to *yourself* about why this bothers you.** Is it the *Hereditary* association? Social comparisons? Fear she’s " different"? Address *your* feelings, not her hobby. - **Ask her: " I miss our conversations. Can we set aside time to just talk about * your* world? I want to understand what you love about miniatures."** - **Support her passion:** Help her find a local miniature art group, a class, or even a part-time job related to it ( e.g., a craft store). This could * actually* look great on a resume. - **Remember:** A " good parent" doesn’t dictate hobbies—they * listen* and * encourage* their child’s unique path. **You’re not the asshole for * caring*— you’re the asshole for * trying to control her* to feel better about yourself.** Fix * your* part of the problem, not hers. 💡
